<pb n="113"/>It is illogical. To this, it is said: "Since that person is not something other than suffering, and since suffering is created by suffering, it is said in one sense that suffering is self-created. Since that which is suffering is not the person, it is also said in another sense that suffering is created by another." To this, it is explained:

Suffering is not self-created,
For it was not created by that very thing.

First, the claim that suffering is self-created in one sense is illogical. Why? Because it was not created by that very same thing <note>the self cannot act upon itself as both subject and object</note>. One must also examine the claim that suffering is created by another in a different sense:

If the other were not self-created,
How could suffering be created by another?

If that which is fixated upon as "another" were not itself created and established, how could that suffering be created by another? To this, it is said: "Suffering exists as something created by the combination of both self and other." To this, it is explained:

If it were created by each one,
Then suffering would be created by both.

If it were the case that it was created by each one <note>individually</note>, then it would follow that suffering is created by both. Since that is not the case, suffering created by the combination of both self and other also does not exist. To this, it is said: "If it is unreasonable for it to be created by self, other, or both, then suffering must arise without a cause." To this, it is explained:

If it is not created by another or by self,
How could suffering be causeless?

If it is not created by another and not created by self, how could it be reasonable for suffering to arise without a cause? This would result in a great logical fallacy.

Not only are the four modes
Non-existent for suffering,
But for external things as well,
Those four modes do not exist.

For the aggregates of suffering alone, those four modes—arising from self, other, both, or without cause— <pb n="114"/> are not only non-existent, but for external things such as form and so on, those four modes also do not exist.

This concludes the twelfth chapter, the Examination of Suffering.

To this, it is said: "Even if those four modes do not exist, suffering and external things, the conditioned phenomena <note>original: <term>saṃskāra</term></note>, do exist." To this, it is explained:

Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false,
So the Blessed One has said.
All conditioned phenomena are deceptive,
Therefore, they are false.

Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the sūtras: "Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false. Monks, it is like this: Nirvana, the non-deceptive phenomenon, is the supreme truth." Because of this, since all conditioned phenomena are deceptive, they are false. Because they appear mistakenly, their imagined essence is empty. To this, it is said: "If whatever conditioned phenomena are deceptive are false, then since both are similar in meaning to non-existence, how can the deceptive nature establish falsehood?" To this, it is explained:

If whatever is deceptive
Is false, what is there to be deceived?
The Blessed One said this
To fully demonstrate emptiness.

If it is said that whatever is deceptive is false, and they are similar in meaning to non-existence, then what would be deceived? Deception is a mistaken appearance, while falsehood refers to the emptiness of the imagined essence; since this is not the same as total non-existence, it is appropriate to establish falsehood through deceptive phenomena. Therefore, one should understand that when the Blessed One spoke of "deceptive phenomena," he was fully demonstrating emptiness. To this, it is said:

Things lack inherent existence,
Because change is seen.

When the Blessed One spoke of "falsehood," it did not mean non-existence or the selflessness of phenomena; rather, it meant that things lack an inherent nature <note>original: <term>svabhāva</term></note> in terms of a person. Why? Because we see things <pb n="115"/> changing into other states.

Without inherent existence, there are no things,
Because all things are empty.

There are no things that lack the inherent existence of phenomena. Why? Because if things are empty, it is illogical for the inherent existence of phenomena to exist.

If inherent existence does not exist,
To what does "change" belong?

If the inherent existence of phenomena does not exist, then to what would the appearance of changing into other states belong? Therefore, when the Blessed One spoke of "falsehood," he meant that things lack the inherent nature of a person, not that the inherent existence of phenomena does not exist. To this, it is explained:

If inherent existence existed,
How could it ever change?

If the inherent existence of phenomena existed, how could it change? For that which is inherent cannot undergo transformation. Furthermore:

There is no change in that very thing,
Nor is there change in something else.
For the youth does not age,
And the aged does not age.

For those who accept the existence of things, there are two types of change: either that very thing changes, or something else changes. Neither is logical. Why? Because a youth <note>while still a youth</note> does not age, and one who is already aged does not age <note>having already aged</note>. To this, it is said: "If that very thing changes into something else, what fault would there be?" To this, it is explained:

If this very thing changed,
Then milk itself would be curd.

If that very thing were to change into something else, then milk itself would be curd; such a thing is illogical. If you think that something else changes into another thing, it is explained:

What thing other than milk
Could possibly be curd?

If you think that something else changes into another, then what thing other than milk could become curd? Therefore, it is illogical for change to occur in either way. To this, it is said: "Is 'emptiness' then the ultimate limit?" To this, it is explained:

If there were something slightly non-empty,
There would be something slightly empty.
Since there is nothing even slightly non-empty,
How could there be anything empty?

<pb n="116"/> If there were something even slightly non-empty, then its antidote, the "empty," would also slightly exist. Since nothing non-empty is accepted, and its antidote is thus absent, how could the empty exist? Furthermore:

The Victors have taught that emptiness
Is the definitive exit from all views.
Those who hold emptiness as a view
Are said to be incurable.

The Buddha, the Blessed Ones, taught that emptiness is the exit from all views because it is the antidote to all views. Thus, those who hold emptiness itself as a view are said to be incurable, like someone putting a skull on top of a meditator's head <note>an idiom for an unnecessary or obstructive addition</note>.

This concludes the thirteenth chapter, the Examination of Reality <note>original: <term>tattva</term></note>.

The Fourth Volume. To this, it is said: "Things definitely have inherent existence, because contact <note>original: <term>saṃsarga</term></note> is seen in the world." To this, it is explained: Previously, in the examination of the faculties, it was shown to be illogical for the three—the object to be seen, the seeing, and the seer—to function. Because they lack otherness, it will now be shown how it is illogical for them to meet or not meet with one another. By what reasoning? It is explained:

The object seen, the seeing, and the seer—
These three, in pairs
Or all together,
Do not meet with one another.

The "object to be seen" refers to the sense objects. "Seeing" refers to the sense faculty. The "seer" refers to the self. These three—the object, the seeing, and the seer—do not meet in pairs or all together. The object and the seeing do not meet; the object and the seer do not meet; the seeing and the seer do not meet; and all three together—object, seeing, and seer—do not meet, just like a lamp and darkness.

Likewise, passion, the one who feels passion,
The object of passion, the afflictions,
And the remaining elements,
Should be viewed in these three ways.

Just as the object, seeing, and seer do not meet in pairs or all together, <pb n="117"/> likewise passion, the one who feels passion, and the object of passion do not meet in pairs or all together. Passion and the one who feels it do not meet; passion and the object of passion do not meet; the one who feels it and the object do not meet; and all three—passion, the feeler, and the object—do not meet. Likewise, the remaining afflictions like hatred, and the remaining sense fields <note>original: <term>āyatana</term></note> like sound and the hearer, should be viewed in these three ways: they do not meet in pairs or all together. To this, it is said: "Why do the object and so on not meet with one another?" To this, it is explained:

If another meets with another,
Since in the object and so on
That otherness does not exist,
They do not meet.

If one holds that these meet because they are "other" than each other, when the object and so on are analyzed through reasoning, that otherness does not exist; therefore, they do not meet. Furthermore:

Not only does otherness not exist
In the object and so forth,
But anything whatsoever
Is illogical as being "other" to another.

Not only is otherness between the object and so on illogical, but no thing whatsoever is logical as being "other" to another thing. If otherness does not exist, then it is illogical for anything to meet with anything else. To this, it is said: "By what reasoning is otherness illogical?" To this, it is explained:

The other is other in dependence on another;
Without the other, the other is not other than the other.
That which exists <pb n="118"/> in dependence on something
Is illogical as being other than that.

That which you fixate upon as "other" becomes "other" only in dependence on some other thing; without that other, it would not be other than itself. Furthermore, that which arises in dependence on something is illogical as being other than it. To this, it is said: "If it were other, what fault would follow?" To this, it is explained:

If the other were other than the other,
It would be so even without the other.
But since that otherness from another
Does not exist, it does not exist.

If that which becomes "other" in dependence on something were indeed other than it, then it would be appropriate for it to be other even without that thing; but that is illogical. If you think that the other is other in dependence on another, then since the otherness from another does not exist, the "other" itself does not exist; therefore, know that there is no otherness. To this, it is said: "Dependent origination is indeed not otherness, but it becomes other in relation to the general category of 'otherness'." To this, it is explained:

Otherness does not exist in the other,
Nor does it exist in the non-other.
If otherness does not exist,
Neither the other nor that very thing exists.

When you say it becomes "other" in relation to the general category of "otherness," are you not simply describing dependent origination? Furthermore, since "otherness" itself is established in dependence and relation to things, it does not exist apart from things, nor does it exist in what is not other. If otherness does not exist, then neither the "other" nor "that very thing" <note>the self-same</note> exist as separate analytical categories. Furthermore:

That very thing does not meet with itself,
Nor does the other meet with the other.
The meeting, the met, <pb n="119"/>
And the meeter do not exist.

That very thing does not meet with itself. Why? Because they are one; that very thing cannot meet with itself. The other does not meet with the other. Why? Because they are distinct; distinct things are not desired to meet, and there is no purpose for it. Thus, since meeting is illogical when things are analyzed, the process of meeting, the object met, and the agent who meets do not exist, just like the sky and the earth.

This concludes the fourteenth chapter, the Examination of Contact.

To this, it is said: "Things definitely have inherent existence, because they are seen to be capable of performing their respective functions, and likewise the inherent nature of a pot or a cloth arises from causes and conditions." To this, it is explained:

It is illogical for inherent existence
To arise from causes and conditions.

It is illogical for inherent existence to arise from causes and conditions. If one thinks, "If inherent existence were to arise from causes and conditions, what fault would there be?" it is explained:

Inherent existence arising
From causes and conditions would be a product.

If it arose from causes and conditions, there would be the fault of inherent existence being a "product" <note>something created</note>. To this, it is said: "If inherent existence were a product, what of it?" To this, it is said:

How could it be appropriate
To call inherent existence a "product"?
Inherent existence is non-fabricated
And independent of anything else.

How could it be appropriate to call inherent existence a "product"? For inherent existence is that which is not fabricated and does not depend on anything else. To this, it is said: "If inherent existence does not exist, then the 'existence of another' <note>original: <term>parabhāva</term></note> must exist." To this, it is explained:

If inherent existence does not exist,
How can the existence of another exist?
The inherent existence of another
Is what is called the "existence of another."

If inherent existence does not exist, how can the existence of another exist? For what is called the "existence of another" <pb n="120"/> is simply the inherent existence of that other. Since that inherent existence is found to be illogical upon analysis, the existence of another also does not exist. To this, it is said: "Even without inherent existence or the existence of another, things <note>original: <term>bhāva</term></note> exist." To this, it is explained:

Apart from inherent existence and other-existence,
How can things exist?
If inherent existence and other-existence
Existed, things would be established.

How can things exist apart from inherent existence and other-existence? Why? Because if inherent existence and other-existence existed, then things would be established. To this, it is said: "Then non-existence <note>original: <term>abhāva</term></note> exists." To this, it is explained:

If things are not established,
Non-existence will not be established.
Ordinary people say that the change of a thing
Is "non-existence."

If the existence of things is not established, then non-existence cannot be established either. Why? Because ordinary people say that when a thing changes into something else, that is "non-existence." To this, it is said: "By seeing the reality of things here, one will be liberated; therefore, the inherent existence of things exists." To this, it is explained:

Those who see inherent existence, other-existence,
Existence, and non-existence,
Do not see the reality
In the Buddha's teaching.

Those who view things in these four modes—inherent existence, other-existence, existence, and non-existence—do not see the reality in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One. Furthermore:

The Blessed One, in the "Advice to Katyayana,"
Which teaches existence and non-existence,
Refuted both
The "it is" and "it is not."

The Blessed One, through the sūtra called the "Advice to Katyayana," which explains existence and non-existence, refuted both "existence" and "non-existence." Therefore...
</translation>

<summary>This passage uses Madhyamaka dialectics to refute the inherent existence of suffering, conditioned phenomena, and the concepts of self and other. It argues that since all things are deceptive and subject to change, they lack an independent essence, and even the concept of emptiness is an antidote rather than a view to be held.</summary>

<keywords>Madhyamaka, emptiness, sunyata, inherent existence, svabhava, dependent origination, Katyayana sutra, suffering, contact, change, Buddhist philosophy, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

If that which is fixated upon as "another" were not itself created and established, how could that suffering be created by another? To this, it is said: "Suffering exists as something created by the combination of both self and other." To this, it is explained:

If it were created by each one,
Then suffering would be created by both.

If it were the case that it was created by each one <note>individually</note>, then it would follow that suffering is created by both. Since that is not the case, suffering created by the combination of both self and other also does not exist. To this, it is said: "If it is unreasonable for it to be created by self, other, or both, then suffering must arise without a cause." To this, it is explained:

If it is not created by another or by self,
How could suffering be causeless?

If it is not created by another and not created by self, how could it be reasonable for suffering to arise without a cause? This would result in a great logical fallacy.

Not only are the four modes
Non-existent for suffering,
But for external things as well,
Those four modes do not exist.

For the aggregates of suffering alone, those four modes—arising from self, other, both, or without cause—
pages.tail: are not only non-existent, but for external things such as form and so on, those four modes also do not exist.

pages.span:
are not only non-existent, but for external things such as form and so on, those four modes also do not exist.

This concludes the twelfth chapter, the Examination of Suffering.

To this, it is said: "Even if those four modes do not exist, suffering and external things, the conditioned phenomena <note>original: <term>saṃskāra</term></note>, do exist." To this, it is explained:

Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false,
So the Blessed One has said.
All conditioned phenomena are deceptive,
Therefore, they are false.

Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the sūtras: "Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false. Monks, it is like this: Nirvana, the non-deceptive phenomenon, is the supreme truth." Because of this, since all conditioned phenomena are deceptive, they are false. Because they appear mistakenly, their imagined essence is empty. To this, it is said: "If whatever conditioned phenomena are deceptive are false, then since both are similar in meaning to non-existence, how can the deceptive nature establish falsehood?" To this, it is explained:

If whatever is deceptive
Is false, what is there to be deceived?
The Blessed One said this
To fully demonstrate emptiness.

If it is said that whatever is deceptive is false, and they are similar in meaning to non-existence, then what would be deceived? Deception is a mistaken appearance, while falsehood refers to the emptiness of the imagined essence; since this is not the same as total non-existence, it is appropriate to establish falsehood through deceptive phenomena. Therefore, one should understand that when the Blessed One spoke of "deceptive phenomena," he was fully demonstrating emptiness. To this, it is said:

Things lack inherent existence,
Because change is seen.

When the Blessed One spoke of "falsehood," it did not mean non-existence or the selflessness of phenomena; rather, it meant that things lack an inherent nature <note>original: <term>svabhāva</term></note> in terms of a person. Why? Because we see things
pages.head: For the aggregates of suffering alone, those four modes—arising from self, other, both, or without cause—

pages.span:
changing into other states.

Without inherent existence, there are no things,
Because all things are empty.

There are no things that lack the inherent existence of phenomena. Why? Because if things are empty, it is illogical for the inherent existence of phenomena to exist.

If inherent existence does not exist,
To what does "change" belong?

If the inherent existence of phenomena does not exist, then to what would the appearance of changing into other states belong? Therefore, when the Blessed One spoke of "falsehood," he meant that things lack the inherent nature of a person, not that the inherent existence of phenomena does not exist. To this, it is explained:

If inherent existence existed,
How could it ever change?

If the inherent existence of phenomena existed, how could it change? For that which is inherent cannot undergo transformation. Furthermore:

There is no change in that very thing,
Nor is there change in something else.
For the youth does not age,
And the aged does not age.

For those who accept the existence of things, there are two types of change: either that very thing changes, or something else changes. Neither is logical. Why? Because a youth <note>while still a youth</note> does not age, and one who is already aged does not age <note>having already aged</note>. To this, it is said: "If that very thing changes into something else, what fault would there be?" To this, it is explained:

If this very thing changed,
Then milk itself would be curd.

If that very thing were to change into something else, then milk itself would be curd; such a thing is illogical. If you think that something else changes into another thing, it is explained:

What thing other than milk
Could possibly be curd?

If you think that something else changes into another, then what thing other than milk could become curd? Therefore, it is illogical for change to occur in either way. To this, it is said: "Is 'emptiness' then the ultimate limit?" To this, it is explained:

If there were something slightly non-empty,
There would be something slightly empty.
Since there is nothing even slightly non-empty,
How could there be anything empty?
pages.head: Because we see things

pages.span:
If there were something even slightly non-empty, then its antidote, the "empty," would also slightly exist. Since nothing non-empty is accepted, and its antidote is thus absent, how could the empty exist? Furthermore:

The Victors have taught that emptiness
Is the definitive exit from all views.
Those who hold emptiness as a view
Are said to be incurable.

The Buddha, the Blessed Ones, taught that emptiness is the exit from all views because it is the antidote to all views. Thus, those who hold emptiness itself as a view are said to be incurable, like someone putting a skull on top of a meditator's head <note>an idiom for an unnecessary or obstructive addition</note>.

This concludes the thirteenth chapter, the Examination of Reality <note>original: <term>tattva</term></note>.

The Fourth Volume. To this, it is said: "Things definitely have inherent existence, because contact <note>original: <term>saṃsarga</term></note> is seen in the world." To this, it is explained: Previously, in the examination of the faculties, it was shown to be illogical for the three—the object to be seen, the seeing, and the seer—to function. Because they lack otherness, it will now be shown how it is illogical for them to meet or not meet with one another. By what reasoning? It is explained:

The object seen, the seeing, and the seer—
These three, in pairs
Or all together,
Do not meet with one another.

The "object to be seen" refers to the sense objects. "Seeing" refers to the sense faculty. The "seer" refers to the self. These three—the object, the seeing, and the seer—do not meet in pairs or all together. The object and the seeing do not meet; the object and the seer do not meet; the seeing and the seer do not meet; and all three together—object, seeing, and seer—do not meet, just like a lamp and darkness.

Likewise, passion, the one who feels passion,
The object of passion, the afflictions,
And the remaining elements,
Should be viewed in these three ways.

Just as the object, seeing, and seer do not meet in pairs or all together,
pages.tail: likewise passion, the one who feels passion, and the object of passion do not meet in pairs or all together.

pages.span:
likewise passion, the one who feels passion, and the object of passion do not meet in pairs or all together. Passion and the one who feels it do not meet; passion and the object of passion do not meet; the one who feels it and the object do not meet; and all three—passion, the feeler, and the object—do not meet. Likewise, the remaining afflictions like hatred, and the remaining sense fields <note>original: <term>āyatana</term></note> like sound and the hearer, should be viewed in these three ways: they do not meet in pairs or all together. To this, it is said: "Why do the object and so on not meet with one another?" To this, it is explained:

If another meets with another,
Since in the object and so on
That otherness does not exist,
They do not meet.

If one holds that these meet because they are "other" than each other, when the object and so on are analyzed through reasoning, that otherness does not exist; therefore, they do not meet. Furthermore:

Not only does otherness not exist
In the object and so forth,
But anything whatsoever
Is illogical as being "other" to another.

Not only is otherness between the object and so on illogical, but no thing whatsoever is logical as being "other" to another thing. If otherness does not exist, then it is illogical for anything to meet with anything else. To this, it is said: "By what reasoning is otherness illogical?" To this, it is explained:

The other is other in dependence on another;
Without the other, the other is not other than the other.
That which exists
pages.head: Just as the object, seeing, and seer do not meet in pairs or all together,
pages.tail:
in dependence on something
Is illogical as being other than that.

pages.span:
in dependence on something
Is illogical as being other than that.

That which you fixate upon as "other" becomes "other" only in dependence on some other thing; without that other, it would not be other than itself. Furthermore, that which arises in dependence on something is illogical as being other than it. To this, it is said: "If it were other, what fault would follow?" To this, it is explained:

If the other were other than the other,
It would be so even without the other.
But since that otherness from another
Does not exist, it does not exist.

If that which becomes "other" in dependence on something were indeed other than it, then it would be appropriate for it to be other even without that thing; but that is illogical. If you think that the other is other in dependence on another, then since the otherness from another does not exist, the "other" itself does not exist; therefore, know that there is no otherness. To this, it is said: "Dependent origination is indeed not otherness, but it becomes other in relation to the general category of 'otherness'." To this, it is explained:

Otherness does not exist in the other,
Nor does it exist in the non-other.
If otherness does not exist,
Neither the other nor that very thing exists.

When you say it becomes "other" in relation to the general category of "otherness," are you not simply describing dependent origination? Furthermore, since "otherness" itself is established in dependence and relation to things, it does not exist apart from things, nor does it exist in what is not other. If otherness does not exist, then neither the "other" nor "that very thing" <note>the self-same</note> exist as separate analytical categories. Furthermore:

That very thing does not meet with itself,
Nor does the other meet with the other.
The meeting, the met,
pages.head: That which exists
pages.tail: And the meeter do not exist.

pages.span:
And the meeter do not exist.

That very thing does not meet with itself. Why? Because they are one; that very thing cannot meet with itself. The other does not meet with the other. Why? Because they are distinct; distinct things are not desired to meet, and there is no purpose for it. Thus, since meeting is illogical when things are analyzed, the process of meeting, the object met, and the agent who meets do not exist, just like the sky and the earth.

This concludes the fourteenth chapter, the Examination of Contact.

To this, it is said: "Things definitely have inherent existence, because they are seen to be capable of performing their respective functions, and likewise the inherent nature of a pot or a cloth arises from causes and conditions." To this, it is explained:

It is illogical for inherent existence
To arise from causes and conditions.

It is illogical for inherent existence to arise from causes and conditions. If one thinks, "If inherent existence were to arise from causes and conditions, what fault would there be?" it is explained:

Inherent existence arising
From causes and conditions would be a product.

If it arose from causes and conditions, there would be the fault of inherent existence being a "product" <note>something created</note>. To this, it is said: "If inherent existence were a product, what of it?" To this, it is said:

How could it be appropriate
To call inherent existence a "product"?
Inherent existence is non-fabricated
And independent of anything else.

How could it be appropriate to call inherent existence a "product"? For inherent existence is that which is not fabricated and does not depend on anything else. To this, it is said: "If inherent existence does not exist, then the 'existence of another' <note>original: <term>parabhāva</term></note> must exist." To this, it is explained:

If inherent existence does not exist,
How can the existence of another exist?
The inherent existence of another
Is what is called the "existence of another."

If inherent existence does not exist, how can the existence of another exist? For what is called the "existence of another"
pages.head: The meeting, the met,
pages.tail: is simply the inherent existence of that other.

pages.span:
is simply the inherent existence of that other. Since that inherent existence is found to be illogical upon analysis, the existence of another also does not exist. To this, it is said: "Even without inherent existence or the existence of another, things <note>original: <term>bhāva</term></note> exist." To this, it is explained:

Apart from inherent existence and other-existence,
How can things exist?
If inherent existence and other-existence
Existed, things would be established.

How can things exist apart from inherent existence and other-existence? Why? Because if inherent existence and other-existence existed, then things would be established. To this, it is said: "Then non-existence <note>original: <term>abhāva</term></note> exists." To this, it is explained:

If things are not established,
Non-existence will not be established.
Ordinary people say that the change of a thing
Is "non-existence."

If the existence of things is not established, then non-existence cannot be established either. Why? Because ordinary people say that when a thing changes into something else, that is "non-existence." To this, it is said: "By seeing the reality of things here, one will be liberated; therefore, the inherent existence of things exists." To this, it is explained:

Those who see inherent existence, other-existence,
Existence, and non-existence,
Do not see the reality
In the Buddha's teaching.

Those who view things in these four modes—inherent existence, other-existence, existence, and non-existence—do not see the reality in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One. Furthermore:

The Blessed One, in the "Advice to Katyayana,"
Which teaches existence and non-existence,
Refuted both
The "it is" and "it is not."

The Blessed One, through the sūtra called the "Advice to Katyayana," which explains existence and non-existence, refuted both "existence" and "non-existence." Therefore...
pages.head: For what is called the "existence of another"
